data: Most famous short-period comet — visible from Earth roughly every 76 years. Edmond Halley correctly predicted its 1759 return based on Newton's gravity, the first such forecast in history. ESA's Giotto flew within 600 km of the nucleus in 1986, returning the first close-up image of a cometary core. Returns next in 2061.
Vega 1 + 2 — USSR, March 1986 (first close imaging on the way to Venus)
Suisei + Sakigake — ISAS, 1986 (Japan’s first interplanetary missions)
Giotto — ESA, 14 March 1986 (closest approach: 596 km; first images of a comet nucleus)
ICE (International Cometary Explorer) — NASA, 1986 (distant tail observations)
Halley's 0.967 eccentricity is the textbook short-period-comet orbit — nearly parabolic, with perihelion 0.59 AU and aphelion 35 AU.
Halley's enormous perihelion-aphelion swing (35 to 0.59 AU) drives the surface ices to sublimate violently near perihelion, producing the coma and tail. Next perihelion: 2061.
How stretched the orbit is — zero is a perfect circle, one is a parabolic escape.
The two extreme points on every elliptical orbit: closest approach, and farthest.
